vignette:
Julian presents as a man accustomed to being in control. At 52, he has built a formidable career as a film director, known for his meticulous visual style and his calm command of chaotic sets. He speaks with a quiet intensity, his hands shaping ideas in the air as if framing a shot. It is this very sense of control, he explains, that he feels has been stolen from him.

The theft occurred ten months ago on a winding mountain road in the Scottish Highlands. He was on a location scout for his next project, a historical drama. He remembers the beauty of it just before everything changed: the bruised purple of the heather, the low-slung clouds, the persistent, drumming rain. He was in the passenger seat of a Jeep, discussing a potential camera angle with the location manager who was driving. He recalls the sickening lurch as the tires lost their grip on the slick asphalt, a moment of weightlessness, and then a violent, cacophonous tumble down a steep embankment.

He speaks of the aftermath in disjointed, sensory fragments. The scream of tearing metal. The smell of gasoline and wet earth. The unnatural silence that followed, broken only by the ticking of the cooling engine and his own ragged breaths. He was suspended upside down by his seatbelt, his arm broken and his head bleeding. It took rescue crews nearly two hours to extract him. The driver did not survive.

Julian's physical recovery was relatively swift. The broken bones healed, the cuts scarred over. He told everyone, including his partner, Anna, that he was lucky. He tried to believe it himself. He threw himself back into pre-production, eager to reclaim the familiar rhythm of his life. But the director was no longer in charge of his own internal world.

Sleep became a minefield. He would wake up gasping, the phantom sensation of falling wrenching him from dreams of twisted metal and shattered glass. During the day, the world was filled with ambushes. A car backfiring on the street would send a jolt of ice through his veins. He stopped driving altogether, claiming the traffic in the city had become unbearable. Anna noticed he would no longer sit in the passenger seat, always insisting on being in the back.

On set, the place that had always been his sanctuary, he felt exposed. The sudden clang of a dropped C-stand made him flinch so violently that the crew would stop and stare. He found himself scanning the high scaffolding and lighting rigs, no longer seeing tools of his trade but potential threats. His famous concentration shattered. While trying to block a scene, the image of the Jeep tumbling end over end would flash behind his eyes, overwriting the story he was trying to tell. He became irritable and withdrawn, his feedback to actors clipped and harsh. The easy collaborative energy he was known for evaporated, replaced by a tense, unpredictable gloom.

At home, he built a wall around the experience. When Anna tried to talk about it, he would change the subject or retreat into his study. He felt a profound sense of detachment, as if he were watching his own life through a camera lens, a distant observer to his own anxiety and grief. The joy he once took in his work, in creating worlds from scratch, has been replaced by a flat, grey exhaustion. He came to therapy after a panic attack during a production meeting, a sudden, overwhelming conviction that the ceiling was about to collapse. It was the first time, he said, that he realized the accident wasn't over. It was still happening, every single day.
